analysis.one_liner: Lets farmers save and replant patented genetically modified seed by paying a government fee instead of royalties.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote and ended the Congress with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: Representative Marcy Kaptur proposed letting farmers who plant patented genetically modified seed keep a portion of their harvested seed to replant, instead of buying new patented seed every year. Farmers would register with the Agriculture Department and pay a fee set by the Secretary into a government fund, and contracts and patent royalties could not stop them from saving seed [S2][S3]. The bill also proposed a new tariff on imported genetically modified seed from countries where the patent owner charges no royalties or lower royalties than in the United States, with the tariff money going into the same fund [S2][S3]. The bill was referred to the House Agriculture and Ways and Means Committees, then sent to the Agriculture subcommittee handling horticulture and biotechnology, and nothing further ever happened [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Farmers who plant patented genetically modified seed. Today, saving and replanting patented seed is barred by seed contracts and patent law, so farmers buy fresh seed each season and pay royalties built into the price [S2][S3]. Under the bill, they could save harvested seed for their own replanting, paying only a fee set by the Secretary of Agriculture into a government fund, and contracts could not stop them [S2][S3]. The bill's sponsors also framed it as increasing seed availability and competition in the seed market [S1][S2].

how_it_helps.text: Farmers could retain harvested genetically modified seed and replant it on their own operations, instead of being contractually and legally required to buy new seed each year [S2][S3].
Contracts and patent fees could not be used to block seed saving; farmers would instead notify the Secretary of Agriculture and pay a government-set fee into a fund [S2][S3].

The bill proposed an additional import duty on genetically modified seed from abroad when the patent owner charges no fees, or lower fees, on that seed than it charges U.S. purchasers, with the duty revenue deposited into the same fund [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Holders of seed patents — the large agricultural biotechnology companies that sell genetically modified seed under patents and licensing contracts — would lose royalty income on seed their customers replanted instead of rebuying. The bill blunts their ability to collect fees on every planting season, and the proposed import tariff would also be borne by importers of foreign-grown genetically modified seed [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection: patent exclusivity is what gives seed companies the incentive to invest in developing new genetically modified varieties in the first place. Letting farmers replant patented seed in exchange for a government-set fee, rather than a royalty the patent holder negotiates, would cut the return on that research and could reduce development of new seed traits [S3].

The replanting fee and the tariff would both be set by executive-branch officials rather than set by law or by negotiation, giving the Agriculture and Treasury Departments substantial discretion over seed markets [S2][S3].
The import duty could raise seed costs for some farmers and would likely raise questions under U.S. trade obligations, since it targets specific foreign seed exports [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a farmer planting patented seed, the benefit is direct: the option to replant saved seed instead of buying new seed every year, paying a government fee rather than the patent holder's royalty [S2][S3]. The cost falls on the seed patent holders, who would lose a large share of the recurring royalties that currently flow to them each season, with some possible loss of research incentives and, from the tariff provision, some higher import costs [S2][S3]. On balance the bill is a transfer of recurring payments from the seed industry to farmers, and it is heavily one-sided in favor of farmers. It died without any committee action or cosponsors, so it never faced an actual test.

outcome.mechanism: The bill sat in House committees — first Agriculture and Ways and Means, then a subcommittee — and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the Congress ended [S5].

narrative.text: Kaptur introduced the bill on January 4, 2013, the first day of the 113th Congress, with no cosponsors [S1][S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Agriculture Committee and, in addition, to the House Ways and Means Committee, which has jurisdiction over tariffs [S5].

On February 4, 2013, it was referred to the Agriculture subcommittee on Horticulture, Research, Biotechnology, and Foreign Agriculture; no further action of any kind was taken for the rest of the Congress [S5].
The bill finished the 113th Congress with zero cosponsors [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The patent-holding seed companies are better off, because the current system — where farmers cannot replant patented seed and must buy new seed and pay royalties each season — remains fully intact. Nothing in law or contract changed.

for.name: Rep. Marcy Kaptur
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; recruited no cosponsors.

against.name: House Agriculture Committee leadership
against.what_they_did: Held the bill in committee and its subcommittee after referral and never scheduled a hearing or markup.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes or cosponsors of any kind, so no party split can be measured; the lone sponsor was a Democrat, and no Republicans or other Democrats joined [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Agricultural biotechnology and patented seed companies
industries.note: These companies earn recurring royalties each season because farmers must buy new patented seed rather than replant saved seed; the bill would have let farmers replant after paying only a government fee, and would have barred contracts and patent fees from blocking seed saving [S2][S3]. Its interest runs against farmers who would save money.
Dealers sell new patented seed to farmers every season; a legal right to replant saved seed would shrink that repeat market [S2][S3].

The bill would have imposed an additional duty on imported genetically modified seed when the patent owner charges no fees, or lower fees, abroad than in the United States, raising costs for importers while directing the revenue to a government fund [S2][S3].
